title: The Woolens Reset: Clean, Inspect, Seal Before Storage
subtitle: A thoughtful end-of-season routine protects the pieces you love—and makes the next change of wardrobe easier.
imageAlt: Two friends prepare wool clothing for storage: one checks a sweater’s seams while the other readies a clean storage container.
imageConcept: A warm, natural-light scene of two friends working side by side at a bedroom table: one turns a wool sweater inside out to inspect its seams, while the other wipes a clean storage bin and folds acid-free tissue nearby.
body: Care is part of getting dressed

The most satisfying seasonal wardrobe change is not simply swapping heavy knits for lighter layers. It is leaving each garment clean, checked and ready for the next time you reach for it. Wool, cashmere, fur and other animal fibers deserve a little more attention before they disappear into a closet or storage box. Clothes-moth larvae—not the adult moths—are the stage that damages fabric, and animal fibers are among the materials they can feed on. Blended fabrics containing animal fibers may also be vulnerable [1].

This is not a reason to treat a wardrobe like a pest-control emergency. It is a practical care routine, much like polishing shoes or checking a coat’s buttons before putting it away. Invite a friend to help: one person can inspect a garment while the other prepares its storage space. The shared task keeps the focus on care, not blame, and makes it easier to notice details you might miss when rushing.
Start with the pieces that need attention

Before folding anything, sort out the garments made wholly or partly from animal fibers: wool sweaters, cashmere scarves, felted accessories, fur-trimmed pieces and similar items. Check the fabric label when you are unsure. You do not need to give every T-shirt or synthetic jacket the same intensive inspection; concentrate on the clothes that are susceptible and that will be stored for a while.

Set aside anything that is visibly soiled or that has been worn close to the skin. Food marks and body oils can make garments more attractive to larvae, and items that go a long time without cleaning or use are more likely to be overlooked [3]. That does not mean a tiny mark guarantees damage. It means the sensible moment to address a stain is before storage, rather than months later when the garment comes back into rotation.

If the piece is secondhand, inspect it before it joins the rest of your wardrobe. The National Pesticide Information Center also advises checking used animal-fiber clothing, rugs and furniture, with particular attention to seams and crevices [2].
Inspect in good light, not at a glance

Choose a bright, uncluttered spot and examine each garment slowly. Turn sweaters inside out. Open collars, cuffs and pockets; spread folds; and look along seams, hems and areas that sit against the body. These tucked-away places can be easy to skip during ordinary dressing, which is why a quick look at the front of a sweater is not a full check [2][3].

Look for irregular holes or surface grazing, along with silken webbing, small cases or larvae. Adult moths are not the fabric-damaging stage, so seeing no fluttering insect is not proof that a garment has been checked [3]. Conversely, a stray hole alone does not identify its cause. The useful habit is to notice and record what you find rather than immediately guessing at a treatment.

If the garment looks intact, move on to cleaning and storage. If you see fresh damage, webbing, larvae or another sign you cannot identify, keep that item separate from the clean pieces and pause the routine. A clear photograph and advice from a local Cooperative Extension office or pest professional are better next steps than treating a delicate garment by guesswork.
Clean according to the garment, not a shortcut

Before long-term storage, clean each vulnerable item in a way its care instructions allow. Read the label and follow the manufacturer’s guidance; wool does not automatically belong in a hot wash. Depending on the garment, the appropriate option may be careful laundering or professional dry-cleaning. The point is to remove soil and address the garment before it sits unused—not to apply one aggressive method to every fiber [1][3].

Treat stains with the same restraint. Follow the care label and the cleaner’s instructions, especially for delicate, structured or valuable pieces. If you are unsure, ask a qualified cleaner rather than experimenting with heat, sprays or home remedies. A garment that needs repair can be mended before storage or placed aside with a clear note to revisit it; otherwise, it is easy for a small snag to become a surprise next season.

Let cleaned items dry fully as directed before packing them away. This is simple wardrobe stewardship: clean first, inspect again as you fold, and avoid sealing in moisture or a forgotten stain.
Reset the drawer or closet, too

A clean garment can be let down by a dusty shelf or a storage bin that still holds lint, hair or debris. Before returning clothes, empty the chosen drawer, closet section or box. Vacuum or wipe the area, paying attention to corners and edges, then make sure it is dry. The reset need not become a full-room deep clean; focus on the space where the susceptible pieces will actually live.

This is a good moment to check that the container is clean and closes securely. If you are using a box or bin that has been in storage, inspect its inside and seams before filling it. Keep the clean garments separate from anything you set aside because of possible activity. The National Pesticide Information Center recommends cleaning before long-term storage and monitoring stored items for signs of moth activity [2].

A deliberate space also makes the wardrobe easier to use. Grouping winter knits together, for instance, means fewer forgotten pieces at the back of a crowded drawer and a more straightforward check when the season changes.
Seal clean garments away—and skip the casual chemical fix

Once a garment is clean, dry and inspected, store it in a tightly closed, airtight container. This is the heart of the routine: do not rely on a scented sachet or a loose cover as a substitute for clean storage. Oregon State University Extension advises cleaning animal-fiber clothing according to its care instructions and storing it in airtight containers [1].

Cedar products are not a dependable guarantee against clothes moths [1]. Mothballs are a different matter altogether: they are pesticides, not a benign closet fragrance. Their use must follow the product label, and they are not meant to be casually placed in an open closet. The vapors can pose risks to people and animals, so do not improvise with them or use them outside label directions [1][2].

If you are considering any pesticide because you have found signs of activity, stop and get reliable identification and guidance first. A preventive wardrobe routine is about cleaning, inspection and secure storage—not layering chemicals onto delicate clothes.
Make the next seasonal change easier

Put the container somewhere you can find it, and make a modest plan to check the garments periodically rather than assuming storage ends the job. When you open the box again, inspect before wearing: look over the fabric and seams, and note anything unusual. Monitoring is part of prevention, not a sign that the routine has failed [2].

For a useful two-person reset, divide the work without turning it into a test. One friend can read care labels and sort pieces into “ready,” “needs cleaning” and “needs advice.” The other can clean the storage area and prepare the container. Then switch roles for the inspection: one holds the garment open while the other checks cuffs, collars, folds and pockets. Keep any questionable item apart from the clean stack, and decide together who will seek identification advice if needed.

The result is more than a protected sweater. It is a wardrobe that has been considered before it disappears from view: cared for on its own terms, stored deliberately and ready to return to your style when the weather turns.
